text.p: Commerzbank AG, Germany's third largest bank, moved on Thursday to quash a frenzy of merger speculation as the bank's shares surged in the third consecutive day of heavy volume trading.
The bank denied rumours that a single large investor was buying up its shares. "You can forget those rumours that there is one large speculative buyer," a Commerzbank spokesman said.

He said the strong rise in the bank's share price was largely due to the fact that the shares were undervalued and said an analysts' meeting held by the bank on Wednesday had been positive, also helping the stock climb.

Commerzbank shares jumped over five percent in extremely heavy pre-bourse electronic trading to hit a new year high of 37.38 marks before paring its gains slightly to end floor dealings at 36.65 marks, up 1.35 marks.

However analysts said merger talk had mainly driven the stock. They agreed that along with most of the rest of the banking sector, Commerzbank shares were indeed undervalued, but said that had been well know for a couple of weeks.
Merger speculation has gripped the German banking sector since July when Deutsche Bank AG said it had amassed a 5.21 percent stake in Munich-based rival Bayerische Vereinsbank AG.
On Thursday, dealers said talk had centred on rumours that Swiss banks were interested in taking over Commmerzbank.

Swiss banking giants Credit Suisse, Swiss Bank Corp. and Union Bank of Switzerland declined to comment on the rumours, which fuelled interest not only in Commerzbank but also in the entire German banking sector.

Over two million Commerzbank shares changed hands in bourse trade and over three million in computer dealings. Meanwhile, four million Deutsche Bank shares traded in computer dealings and the stock rose 1.80 marks to 72.25 marks. Bayerische Vereinsbank was up 39 pfennigs at 62.01 marks.
Despite the furore, analysts said Swiss banks were unlikely to be interested in Commerzbank, which did not have the strength in investment banking known to interest the Swiss.
"I cannot see anyone taking over Commerzbank at the moment, at least not until they have restructured," said Konrad Becker, banking analyst at Merck, Finck in Frankfurt.

Other analysts said they were already impressed with the bank's efforts to cut costs. Commerzbank has cut its cost-income ratio to 64 percent, well below Germany's two largest banks Deutsche Bank and Dresdner Bank.

But Commerzbank's chief executive Martin Kohlhaussen said last week the bank's heavy market capitalisation of 15 billion marks ($9.96 billion) should deter bidders and he could not imagine a buyer paying so much for a branch network in need of restructuring.

Banking mergers have become such a hot topic in German markets that a mere sighting of Kohlhaussen having breakfast in Munich earlier this week was enough to send rumours flying that the bank was in talks on links with Bayerische Vereinsbank.

The talk sparked heavy trading in Commerzbank shares on Tuesday and Wednesday and analysts said Kohlhaussen had commented on this rumour at their Wednesday meeting, confirming that he had indeed been in Munich, but to attend a supervisory board meeting at building group Hochtief AG.
"At the analysts' meeting Kohlhaussen repeated in very definite terms that Commerzbank would not be taken over, nor would it acquire anybody else," said Becker.

But on Thursday the chief executive of Germany's fifth largest bank, Bayerische Hypotheken- und Wechsel- Bank, Eberhard Martini, said all banks had considered the possibility that merger activity could break out in the sector.
"It could well be the current market speculation about mergers will blow over. But we, as managers must be prepared for all eventualities," said Martini.
Some dealers said the dramatic move in Commerzbank shares this week was mainly due to technical factor after the stock broke out of the narrow range it had held since August.
